record.paper_title: Some Open Problems in Quantum Information Theory
record.context_brief: Bell inequalities for finite correlation experiments
record.original_question: In a Bell-type correlation experiment with N subsystems, M measurement choices per subsystem, and K outcomes per measurement, characterize exactly the measured probability tables that admit a classical local realistic joint probability distribution over all NM observables. Equivalently, describe the convex polyhedron generated by all classical configurations in terms of linear Bell inequalities; for tractable cases, find complete solutions for small triples (N, M, K), efficient methods for generating genuinely new inequalities, infinite or symmetry-restricted families, full-correlation-function versions, correlation inequalities for K = 2, and the margins by which such inequalities can be violated by quantum states, possibly under constraints such as fixed Hilbert-space dimension, symmetry, or positive partial transposes.

evidence.quote: Find all those linear inequalities characterizing the existence of joint probability distributions for all variables in a correlation experiment.
More specifically, suppose that measurements are made on systems, which are decomposed into N subsystems. On each of these subsystems one out of M observables is measured, producing K outcomes each.

Decide by what margin these can be violated by quantum states, or by quantum states with special properties (e. g., fixed Hilbert space dimension, invariance under symmetry transformations or positive partial transposes).

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a Bell-type correlation experiment with the following setup. There are $N$ spatially separated subsystems. On each subsystem, an experimenter freely chooses one of $M$ possible measurements, and each measurement yields one of $K$ possible outcomes. A run of the experiment produces, for each choice of one measurement setting per subsystem (an element of $\{1,\dots,M\}^N$), an empirical joint probability distribution over the $K^N$ outcome tuples. Call the collection of all such conditional distributions a "behavior" or probability table.

A behavior is said to admit a local realistic (classical) model if there exists a single joint probability distribution over the values of all $NM$ observables (one for each (subsystem, setting) pair, each taking values in $\{1,\dots,K\}$) whose marginals reproduce the measured conditional distributions for every choice of one setting per subsystem.

The set of local realistic behaviors forms a convex polytope $\mathcal{L}(N,M,K)$ in the appropriate Euclidean space of probability tables, whose vertices are the deterministic local assignments. Its facets are linear inequalities (Bell inequalities).

Problems:
1. (Complete characterization.) Determine the full list of facet-defining linear inequalities of $\mathcal{L}(N,M,K)$ for all triples $(N,M,K)$, or for as many small triples as possible beyond those currently known.
2. (Generation of new inequalities.) Develop efficient algorithmic or constructive methods to produce genuinely new (non-liftable, non-symmetry-equivalent) facet inequalities of $\mathcal{L}(N,M,K)$.
3. (Structured families.) Identify infinite families of facet inequalities, families invariant under prescribed symmetry groups (e.g.\ permutations of parties, settings, or outcomes), and the full-correlation-function inequalities involving only joint expectations of products of $\pm 1$-valued observables when $K=2$.
4. (Quantum violations.) For each such inequality, determine the maximal quantum violation, i.e.\ the supremum of its value over behaviors arising from quantum states and measurements, possibly under restrictions such as fixed Hilbert-space dimension, invariance under specified symmetry groups, or positive partial transpose across given bipartitions.
artifact.status_search_result: The complete facet enumeration of the local (Bell) polytope is a well-known computationally hard problem (facet enumeration on a polytope whose complexity grows roughly as $O((\exp N)^{\exp N})$). Complete lists of facet Bell inequalities are only known in a handful of small cases (e.g., bipartite scenarios with up to four binary settings: 175 facets). General characterization, efficient generation of new inequalities, and determination of maximal quantum violations under structural constraints remain active open research, with recent work focusing on sampling-based, symmetry-restricted, and permutationally invariant techniques.

status_evidence.title: Bell Inequalities from Polyhedral Sampling
status_evidence.snippet: Enumerating all Bell inequalities for a given scenario remains intractable beyond the simplest cases, as it requires solving a computationally hard facet enumeration problem on the associated Bell polytope.
status_evidence.claim: Complete facet enumeration of Bell polytopes is computationally intractable in general.

status_evidence.title: Complete list of tight Bell inequalities for two parties with four binary settings
status_evidence.snippet: The complete list of 175 facets of the local polytope has been determined for the case where Alice and Bob each choose from four binary measurements.
status_evidence.claim: Only small scenarios have a fully known list of facet Bell inequalities.

status_evidence.title: Optimizing quantum violation for multipartite facet Bell inequalities
status_evidence.snippet: As the number of parties increases ... the complexity of characterizing the local polytope grows as O((exp N)^(exp N)), rendering a complete characterization of multipartite nonlocality intractable.
status_evidence.claim: Multipartite local-polytope characterization is intractable; quantum-violation optimization is ongoing research.
